# Pretraining a small time-series foundation model from scratch: a research note

*Generated by `tsfm docs build` from committed results. Every number below is read from
a file under `results/`.*

## Question

Can a small decoder-only transformer, pretrained from scratch only on public data that
we have checked for overlap with the benchmark, forecast unseen series zero-shot better
than classical per-series baselines on GIFT-Eval? How does accuracy change with model
size and compute, and with the choice of tokenizer?

## Data

See `DATA_CARD.md`. Two findings matter for anyone using the same corpus:

1. The upstream pretraining collection, described as non-leaking, contains exact or
   rescaled copies of GIFT-Eval series (Australian weather vs `temperature_rain`, Beijing
   air quality vs `kdd_cup_2018`, several Monash monthly sets and FRED-MD vs `m4_monthly`,
   pedestrian counts vs `m4_hourly`), some inside GIFT-Eval's test windows. We excluded
   every flagged series; numbers are in the data card.
2. A naive window-hash check also produces false matches from linearly interpolated
   gaps, which look identical in every series after normalisation; these must be
   filtered or inspected, not counted as leakage.

## Method

Decoder-only transformer, pre-norm RMSNorm, rotary positions, SwiGLU, KV cache, in plain
PyTorch. Two tokenizers: (a) mean scaling and 4,096-token quantisation with
cross-entropy, sampled autoregressively; (b) patches with a non-crossing quantile head,
rolled out by feeding back medians. Training samples a random context length per window
and computes the scale from the context only. Evaluation follows GIFT-Eval exactly (our
Seasonal Naive reproduces upstream's on all official metrics and configurations).

## Results

### Scaling (validation split)

Power-law fit L = a * C^(-b) over 3 runs: b = 0.0578 (95% bootstrap interval 0.0508 to 0.0636, paired over validation batches).

| run | body params | train FLOPs (6ND) | val loss |
|---|---|---|---|
| patch_s0 | 754,688 | 7.42e+13 | 0.2355 |
| patch_s1 | 2,656,512 | 8.36e+14 | 0.1975 |
| patch_s2 | 9,671,680 | 1.14e+16 | 0.1759 |

![Validation loss against training compute for the patch models. The line is the fitted power law and the band is its paired bootstrap, both read from the committed scaling fit.](docs/figures/scaling.svg)

### Tokenizer comparison at a fixed budget (validation split)

*Not concluded. `bins_s2` was trained at the same size and token budget as `patch_s2`, but its validation scoring (20 sampled paths per window) did not finish within the compute budget, so no tokenizer comparison is reported (`DEVIATIONS.md`).*

### Zero-shot GIFT-Eval (test split)

`patch_s2`, the T4 headline, was scored once on the test split after the deadline, from its checkpoint on Drive (`notebooks/score_patch_s2_test.ipynb`), with the pre-registered settings and one seed (`DEVIATIONS.md`). The first row is the primary comparison.

| model | vs | metric | ratio | 95% CI | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| headline | upstream:Auto_Arima | crps | 0.688 | [0.624, 0.757] | better |
| headline | upstream:Auto_Arima | mase | 0.851 | [0.684, 0.986] | better |
| headline | seasonal_naive | crps | 0.628 | [0.569, 0.692] | better |
| headline | seasonal_naive | mase | 0.914 | [0.848, 0.989] | better |

A smaller model was pre-registered separately (`PREREGISTRATION_CPU.md`) and scored once, three seeds, on all 97 official configurations. Seed-averaged CRPS is 1.109× Seasonal Naive (95% configuration interval [0.978, 1.265], no detectable difference) and 1.217× upstream AutoARIMA (interval entirely above 1, worse).

Official GIFT-Eval test split, 97 configurations, 3 seeds. MASE and CRPS are geometric means of each score divided by Seasonal Naive. The interval next to the ratio is a 95% paired bootstrap over configurations of the seed-averaged scores (10,000 resamples). The other interval is a 95% Student-t interval across seed-level CRPS ratios; with three seeds it is wide on purpose. Conformal expansions were fit on the validation split only. A ratio below 1 is better than Seasonal Naive.

| model | MASE | CRPS | CRPS ratio vs Seasonal Naive [95% config CI] | CRPS ratio across seeds [95% t CI] | 80% coverage | vs Seasonal Naive |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| cpu_s0, raw quantiles | 1.835 | 1.109 | 1.109 [0.978, 1.265] | [0.654, 1.516] | 0.642 | no detectable difference |
| cpu_s0, split-conformal | 1.835 | 1.277 | 1.277 [1.130, 1.455] | [0.603, 1.920] | 0.932 | worse |

Ratio of seed-averaged geometric means, model divided by upstream AutoARIMA, both already divided by Seasonal Naive. Below 1 would be better than AutoARIMA. The pre-registered decision rule: better if the interval is entirely below 1, worse if it is entirely above 1, otherwise no detectable difference.

| model | metric | ratio to AutoARIMA | 95% CI | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| cpu_s0 raw | crps | 1.217 | [1.091, 1.362] | worse |
| cpu_s0 raw | mase | 1.709 | [1.343, 2.088] | worse |
| cpu_s0 split-conformal | crps | 1.401 | [1.249, 1.576] | worse |
| cpu_s0 split-conformal | mase | 1.709 | [1.343, 2.088] | worse |

The same three seeds on the validation split average CRPS 0.988× Seasonal Naive. The test ratio is higher. Nothing was changed after the test scores were written.

Split-conformal expansions were fit per seed on validation forecasts only. On the test split they leave MASE unchanged and move CRPS to 1.277× Seasonal Naive, which is worse. Empirical 80% coverage moves from 0.642 to 0.932. The validation conformal row in the table below reuses the fit set.

### Fine-tuning on realized volatility, and regime robustness

Design fixed in `PREREGISTRATION_VOL.md` (tag `prereg-vol-v1`) before scoring: daily
realized volatility of BTCUSDT and ETHUSDT from Binance Vision 5-minute klines
(CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), 22-day forecasts from every day of the test period, pooled weighted
quantile loss with moving-block bootstrap intervals.

Our model was not run on this study before the deadline; the baselines were.

These are statistical forecast scores only. They say nothing about trading
performance, and none is claimed.

## Scope

`DEVIATIONS.md` records, before any T4 model was scored on the test split, what was
cut from that pre-registered plan: three model sizes instead of four to six, no
tokenizer conclusion, one seed, and no test-split scoring of `patch_s2`. The later CPU
study is a separate pre-registration. It did score its own model once.

## Not established

Things this project does **not** show, whatever the numbers above say:

* That the two test results describe one model. The CPU model
  (833,440 parameters) is separate;
  on it, CRPS against Seasonal Naive is not distinguishable from 1, and both CRPS and
  MASE are worse than upstream AutoARIMA.
* That the CPU result would survive a larger training budget. It is 2,000 steps on CPU.
* That the model is useful for any real forecasting or trading decision. Nothing here
  measures economic value, and no trading performance is claimed.
* That scaling trends continue beyond the sizes trained: the fit describes three runs.
* That the T4 headline holds across training seeds: `patch_s2` was scored with one seed.
  The CPU study has three seeds. Their test CRPS ratios are
  0.935,
  1.045 and
  1.275.
  The mean of those three is
  1.085,
  and the Student-t interval on that mean is
  [0.654,
  1.516].
  That is not the interval on the seed-averaged ratio.
* Which tokenizer is better: the comparison did not complete.
* That the corpus is free of *all* benchmark overlap: the check finds exact and affine
  copies, not noisy, warped or differently aggregated ones.
* That differences within a frequency, domain or horizon group are real: those
  breakdowns are descriptive and not corrected for multiple comparisons.
* That far-horizon intervals of the patch model are calibrated: median roll-outs ignore
  the uncertainty of earlier steps.
* Anything about users or adoption: there are none.
